explain.unemployment: How many people want a job but can't find one. Picture everyone aged 15 to 74 who either has a job or is actively looking for one. The unemployment rate is the share of that group who are looking but don't have a job. If it is 8%, then 8 out of every 100 people in that group are without work and searching. People who aren't looking for work, like most students and retired people, aren't counted at all. Lower is better.
explain.inflation: How fast prices are rising. It compares this year's average prices of everyday things, like food, rent, electricity and transport, with last year's. At 2%, a shopping basket that cost 100 euros last year costs 102 euros this year. A number below zero means prices fell. Most European central banks aim for about 2%, so very high numbers and negative numbers are both a warning sign. The ranking puts the lowest number first, even though falling prices aren't good either. Eurostat calls this measure HICP.
explain.gdp_per_capita: How rich a country is per person. It adds up the value of everything produced in the country in a year and divides it by the number of people living there. Price differences between countries are evened out, so the comparison shows how much that output could actually buy. The EU average is set to 100: a score of 120 means 20% above the EU average, and 80 means 20% below. Big international companies can push the number up, so it doesn't always match what people there earn. Eurostat says to use it for comparing countries in the same year, not for following one country over time. Higher is better.
explain.at_risk_of_poverty: How many people have a lot less money than most people in their own country. Line up everyone in a country by income, after taxes and benefits. The person in the very middle has the median income. Anyone with less than 60% of that counts as at risk of poverty. If it is 12%, then 12 out of every 100 people are below that line. Because the line is set separately in each country, it is a much smaller amount of money in a poorer country than in a richer one. Lower is better.
explain.median_income_pps: How much money a typical person has to live on in a year. Line everyone up by income and look at the person in the very middle: that is the median income. It is the money left after taxes and benefits. It is also adjusted for household size: a family of four needs more money than someone living alone, but not four times as much, because they share a home and many other things. PPS evens out price differences between countries, so a higher number really means the money buys more. Higher is better.
explain.median_income_eur: The same typical income as the PPS version, but in plain euros. Prices are not evened out, so it shows the actual amount of money, not what that money can buy. A euro buys a lot more in Bulgaria than in Denmark, so to compare how well people live, use the PPS version. Higher is better.
explain.gini: How evenly money is shared out in a country, as a single number. 0 would mean everyone has exactly the same income. 100 would mean one person gets all of it. Every real country is somewhere in between: among the countries here, recent figures go from about 22 (Slovakia) to about 38 (Bulgaria). A lower number means incomes are more equal. It says nothing about whether people are rich or poor overall, only how evenly the money is spread. Rank 1 is the most equal country.
explain.life_expectancy: How long a baby born in a given year can expect to live, on average. It is calculated as if that year's death rates stayed the same for the baby's whole life, so it is an estimate, not a prediction. It goes up when health care gets better, life gets safer and habits get healthier. In Finland it was about 82 years in 2024. Higher is better.
explain.pisa_math: PISA is a test taken by 15-year-olds in dozens of countries, usually every three years. The newest results here are from 2022. The maths part asks students to use maths in everyday situations, like working out prices or reading a chart. Each country gets an average score. In the EU in 2022, scores went from 417 (Bulgaria) to 510 (Estonia). A difference of a few points is within the margin of error. PISA has no EU average, so the OECD average is shown instead. The OECD is a group of 38 mostly wealthy countries. Higher is better.
explain.pisa_reading: The reading part of PISA, the test for 15-year-olds. Students read things like news articles, messages and instructions. Then they find information in them, work out what is meant and judge whether the text can be trusted. As with maths, a difference of a few points is within the margin of error, and the OECD average is shown for comparison. Higher is better.
explain.pisa_science: The science part of PISA, the test for 15-year-olds. Students explain things that happen in nature, judge how an experiment was set up and use evidence to reach a conclusion. As with maths, a difference of a few points is within the margin of error, and the OECD average is shown for comparison. Higher is better.
